Releasing is fully automated end to end, including the version number itself — a PR never needs to touch package.json or the version in docs/contract.md. CHANGELOG.md is different: the release writes the version heading and one line per merged PR, but a feat PR writes its own notes under ## Unreleased (CONTRIBUTING.md), and a PR that closes an issue must name that issue in CHANGELOG.md or test_changelog_mentions_every_closed_issue_since_last_tag fails. Once a PR merges to main, .github/workflows/release.yml takes it from there: if nobody bumped the version by hand, it resolves the next version with .github/scripts/resolve_version.py. What that script reads, its rules, their exceptions and the incidents behind them are written once, in its docstring, and test_release_version_resolver_rules and test_release_version_resolver_does_not_depend_on_a_pr_title pin them; they are not restated here. Most PRs don't need a label added by hand: release-drafter.yml's autolabel job applies one automatically from the PR's title/changed files (Fix ... → fix, Add .../feat ... → feature, docs/.md/.github//build(deps) changes → chore) as soon as it's opened — add a label yourself only to override that. A major version is never chosen automatically: no label rule produces major, and the workflow refuses to auto-bump across a major boundary even if someone applies that label — a real major release is a deliberate package.json bump in a PR, which the manual path below already handles. It bumps package.json, .claude-plugin/plugin.json, docs/contract.md and docs/roadmap.md's released-version sentence, writes a CHANGELOG.md section listing those PRs (and any issues they closed), and pushes that commit to main itself. If another PR merged while the bump was being prepared, the push is refused and that run releases nothing: the newer merge's own run, queued behind it, starts from main's tip and releases both (the bump is never rebased onto a merge it did not read). After the tag it also asks pages.yml to rebuild the site, because the bump commit carries [skip ci] and would otherwise leave the site on the previous version. Either way — auto-bumped or hand-bumped in the PR — it then creates the vX.Y.Z tag, publishes a GitHub Release with notes extracted from CHANGELOG.md's matching section, and publishes the package to npm. A PR that still wants to write its own version bump and CHANGELOG.md prose (e.g. to explain the "why" of a release by hand) can — the automation only fills in when nobody made that call already. A push to main with nothing new to release creates no tag, Release or npm publish; its MCP Registry step still asks npm and the registry about server.json's version and publishes the entry only when npm has that version and the registry does not, which is how a later run finishes an entry an earlier one failed to publish. npm publishing needs an NPM_TOKEN repo secret (an npm access token with publish rights on this package) — without it the tag and GitHub Release still happen, only the npm step is skipped. A repo that depends on this one (an editing skill, an agent) should pin an ffmpeg-skill version by tag or npm version, not by tracking main — a merged-but-not-yet-released commit on main can be ahead of the last published npm version for the few minutes between merge and this workflow completing.

A version that was tagged but never reached npm (the npm step failed; a re-run of that release sees the tag and skips the publish) is finished by dispatching the same workflow on its tag: gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f version=X.Y.Z. That runs only the workflow's recover job. It refuses a version that is not X.Y.Z, has no tag, or that npm already has, and a run whose commit is not the tagged one: the npm provenance attestation names the run's commit, so it must be the commit the package is built from. It publishes with --provenance under the latest dist-tag when the version is above every stable (non-prerelease) version npm has, and under backport otherwise, so latest never moves back. Then it publishes the plugin branch when no commit there is for this version and the branch's tip is older, and the MCP Registry entry when the registry does not list the version (never for a backport). The GitHub Release is left as it is. A tag cut before the job was added (#448; every tag up to v3.6.3) has no recover job at its commit and cannot be recovered this way.

Contributing a change: see CONTRIBUTING.md.

Support

If this skill saves you time, you can help keep it maintained through GitHub Sponsors. Issues and pull requests are just as welcome.

Builds with GPL components such as libx264, libx265 or libvidstab use GPL terms. That affects the default x264/x265 encoding paths and the vid.stab filters used by stabilize.py. FFmpeg labels builds configured with --enable-nonfree as non-redistributable. doctor displays the license reported by the selected executable. See FFmpeg's license and distribution information.

item.title: vercel-labs/agent-browser
item.description:
Browser automation CLI for AI agents

https://agent-browser.dev

agent-browser

Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell.

agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call.

Install

npm install -g agent-browser
agent-browser install           # download Chrome for Testing (first time only)
  • Homebrew: brew install agent-browser, then agent-browser install.
  • Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries.
  • No install: npx agent-browser open example.com.

Project installs, building from source, upgrade, and doctor are covered in Installation.

Quick start

agent-browser open example.com
agent-browser snapshot -i       # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-browser click @e1         # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-browser get url           # check the result
agent-browser close

The snapshot for example.com:

- link "Learn more" [ref=e1]
  • Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again.
  • CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit". See Selectors.
  • A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry.

The full walkthrough is in the quick start.

How it works

The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured.

Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect (CDP mode), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine, drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator, or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase, Browserless, Browser Use, Kernel, or AgentCore.

For AI agents

The CLI ships skills that match its version:

agent-browser skills get core                 # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows
agent-browser skills get core --ref commands  # one reference, such as the full command list
agent-browser skills get core --full          # adds the full command reference and templates
agent-browser skills list                     # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more

Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from skills.sh:

npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser

The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load agent-browser skills get core, so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add this to your AGENTS.md:

Use `agent-browser` for browser automation. Before the first use, run
`agent-browser skills get core` and follow it.

For MCP clients, agent-browser mcp starts an MCP server over stdio. See MCP server.

Commands

Run agent-browser --help for the full list, or agent-browser <command> --help for one command.

Group Commands Docs
Navigate and read open, back, forward, reload, read, snapshot, get, is Core, Snapshots
Interact click, dblclick, fill, type, press, keyboard, hover, focus, select, check, uncheck, scroll, drag, upload, mouse, find Core, Find elements
Wait wait Wait
Capture screenshot, pdf, record, download, diff Recording, Diffing, Files
Page and network state cookies, storage, network, set, clipboard, eval, pushstate Network, Settings
Tabs, frames, and dialogs tab, frame, dialog Tabs and frames
Debug and performance console, errors, highlight, inspect, trace, profiler, vitals, react, a11y Debugging, Profiler, React
Sessions and auth session, state, auth, profiles, confirm, deny Sessions, Security
Agents and integrations skills, mcp, webmcp, flow, chat, batch, plugin Skills, WebMCP, Plugins
Observe stream, dashboard Streaming, Dashboard
Setup install, upgrade, doctor, connect, close Installation

Flags, environment variables, and agent-browser.json are documented in Configuration.

Platforms

Native binaries ship for macOS (ARM64, x64), Linux (ARM64, x64, glibc and musl), and Windows (x64). The npm package picks the right binary for the host.

Development

Building from source requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust:

pnpm install
pnpm build:source               # builds the dashboard and the native CLI
pnpm link --global
agent-browser install

Run the Rust checks from cli/:

cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy
cargo test
cargo test e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1   # launches real headless Chrome

AGENTS.md lists the files to update with each change, the docs checks, and the release process.

Documentation

  • agent-browser.dev: introduction, guides, and reference
  • Commands and Configuration
  • Security: the auth vault, domain allowlists, action policies, and content boundaries
  • Next.js and Vercel and eve: running agent-browser in Vercel Sandbox and eve agents
  • Changelog
